analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of unauthorized bank accounts and credit cards sue in court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 21 Democratic and independent senators, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 2017-2019 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After Wells Fargo employees opened more than 2 million fake customer accounts, the bank used the fine-print arbitration clauses on customers' legitimate accounts to keep fraud victims out of court. This bill would make forced-arbitration clauses unenforceable for disputes involving a credit card or bank account that the customer never asked for, letting those victims sue in court instead. It never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers hit with accounts or cards they never opened, and other victims of fraud on accounts they did not request, would be able to take their claims to a judge or jury rather than a private arbitrator. The bill's findings cite Wells Fargo customers who were forced into arbitration over fake accounts even after the bank admitted the conduct.

how_it_helps.text: Bars forced-arbitration clauses from being enforced in any dispute over a credit card account that was not opened in response to a customer's request or application [S3].
Applies the same bar to personal deposit and asset accounts opened without the customer's request, restoring access to state and federal court for those disputes [S3].

The bill's findings document that courts repeatedly held Wells Fargo's customers bound to arbitration over fraud on accounts they never opened, citing over 1.5 million unauthorized checking accounts and 565,443 unauthorized credit card accounts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit card issuers lose the ability to funnel fraud claims on unauthorized accounts into arbitration, where private arbitrators and confidential proceedings replace public court records. Arbitration providers lose the associated business.

drawbacks.text: The protection is narrow: it applies only to accounts the customer never requested, so the standard arbitration clause in the ordinary credit card or bank account agreement remains fully enforceable for every other kind of dispute [S3].

Banking and arbitration defenders argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper for small-dollar claims, and that keeping those disputes out of class actions benefits the lawyers who bring them more than the customers — the same trade-off at issue in the CFPB's broader arbitration rule fight of the same Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real but limited: millions of Wells Fargo-style fraud victims regain their day in court, at the cost of banks handling those specific claims in court rather than a private forum. The bill does nothing about the much larger universe of arbitration clauses covering disputes on accounts customers did open, so the case-by-case cost to banks is modest and the benefit is targeted rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which under a Republican chairman never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on March 7, 2017, joined by 20 Democratic and 1 independent cosponsor, in the months after the Wells Fargo fake-accounts scandal [S1, S4, S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever appears in its action history [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and card issuers kept the arbitration clauses that send fraud claims over unauthorized accounts into private arbitration, sparing them the courtroom exposure this bill would have created. Arbitration providers keep the business.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio, bill sponsor, Banking Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 20 Democratic and 1 independent cosponsors; as the Banking Committee's ranking Democrat, watched it go nowhere under the chairman.

for.name: 21 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 20 Democrats and 1 independent, including Leahy, Warren, Sanders, Durbin, and Wyden

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Banking Committee gave the bill no action beyond referral.

industries.note: The bill strips the arbitration clauses that let issuers send fraud claims on accounts customers never opened into a private forum instead of court. Banks' interest in keeping those claims out of court runs against the fraud victims' interest in suing.
Private arbitration providers would lose fees on credit card and bank account disputes over unauthorized accounts. Their business model depends on the mandatory clauses the bill makes unenforceable.
The bill reopens a courtroom path for fraud victims on unauthorized accounts, restoring the kind of claims these firms bring on contingency. Customers only recover when they can hire representation.
